scope: Rules are applied to NAICS sectors and 3-digit subsectors together, so a subsector can appear alongside its parent sector. QCEW private ownership.

findings.question: What appears distinctive about Detroit's industrial structure?
findings.rule: Detroit LQ ≥ 1.25 with at least 1,000 jobs, while Chicago and Cleveland both have LQ < 1.0.
findings.text: No industry meets the rule in the selected end year.

findings.question: Which strengths are shared across the three metros?
findings.rule: LQ ≥ 1.1 in all three metros, each with at least 1,000 jobs.
findings.text: No industry is specialized (by this rule) in all three metros.

findings.question: Which industries combine specialization with positive growth?
findings.rule: End-year LQ ≥ 1, at least 1,000 jobs, and employment grew over the selected period.
findings.text: Count of qualifying industries by metro. Metro Detroit: 8 — Real estate +22.1%; Credit intermediation and related activities +18.1%; Real estate and rental and leasing +15.8%. Metro Chicago: 3 — Truck transportation +15.9%; Merchant wholesalers, nondurable goods +8.7%; Finance and insurance +5.2%. Greater Cleveland: 9 — Repair and maintenance +14.0%; Insurance carriers and related activities +13.3%; Arts, entertainment, and recreation +10.8%.

findings.question: Where do employment trends suggest vulnerability?
findings.rule: End-year LQ ≥ 1, at least 1,000 jobs, and employment declined over the selected period.
findings.text: Count of qualifying industries by metro. Metro Detroit: 4 — Fabricated metal product manufacturing -19.0%; Plastics and rubber products manufacturing -12.6%; Machinery manufacturing -9.1%. Metro Chicago: 2 — Credit intermediation and related activities -8.6%; Administrative and support and waste management and remediation services -8.1%. Greater Cleveland: 9 — Fabricated metal product manufacturing -12.6%; Chemical manufacturing -7.3%; Machinery manufacturing -6.9%.

findings.question: Does each metro's industry mix appear to favor or constrain its employment growth?
findings.rule: Sum of sector-level shift-share components over sectors with complete data. A positive industry-mix sum means the metro's base-year mix was weighted toward nationally faster-growing sectors.
findings.text: Metro Detroit: industry mix -17,604 jobs, regional effect -87,249 jobs (sectors covering 70% of base-year employment). Metro Chicago: industry mix -106,911 jobs, regional effect -94,579 jobs (sectors covering 27% of base-year employment). Greater Cleveland: industry mix -10,697 jobs, regional effect -119,235 jobs (sectors covering 87% of base-year employment). The regional effect describes relative employment growth only; it does not identify causes.

findings.question: Which differences merit further investigation?
findings.rule: Industries where Detroit's regional effect has the opposite sign from both Chicago's and Cleveland's.
findings.text: Candidates for further study (not explanations): Credit intermediation and related activities (Detroit regional effect +6,478 jobs); Finance and insurance (Detroit regional effect +5,732 jobs); Specialty trade contractors (Detroit regional effect +88 jobs).

findings.question: What do establishment, GDP and workforce measures add?
findings.rule: Reported side by side with their own reference periods; not combined with QCEW employment into a single index.
findings.text: Private establishments per 1,000 private jobs (CBP 2023): Metro Detroit 55.5; Metro Chicago 58.0; Greater Cleveland 53.0. Residents 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher (ACS 2024): Metro Detroit 35.6% ±0.6; Metro Chicago 43.1% ±0.4; Greater Cleveland 34.7% ±0.8. Metro Detroit vs Metro Chicago: statistically different at 90%; Metro Detroit vs Greater Cleveland: not statistically different at 90%; Metro Chicago vs Greater Cleveland: statistically different at 90%.
